 Making history…everywhere on Election Day and beyond! 
 Corner to Corner by Columnist Diane Denish 
 by 
 Diane Denish 
 7 minutes ago

 Corner to Corner by Diane Denish
 Corner to Corner by Columnist Diane D. Denish — This year, I began election week in Chicago with a visit to the Obama Presidential Center. It was the result of a spur-of-the-moment decision in July, when I went online to buy tickets and discovered November 1 was the first available date.
 This year, I began election week in Chicago with a visit to the Obama Presidential Center. It was the result of a spur-of-the-moment decision in July, when I went online to buy tickets and discovered November 1 was the first available date.
 Corner to Corner
 Diane Denish is a former lieutenant governor of New Mexico. She is a native of Hobbs and now lives in Albuquerque.
 At the time, it seemed like a little insurance going into what promised to be a historic election week. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland was on track, barring major missteps or revelations, to become the nation’s first Native American governor.
 I pushed the “buy tickets” icon.
  Revisiting the Obama presidency would reinforce my hopes for what was possible in 2026: a return to decency, protecting democracy and recognizing the power of the people who participate and vote.
 Like others,  I watched this historic election season take shape.
 As the days and weeks progressed, it became clear Deb Haaland would not be the only history maker.
 Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia could become the first Black woman governor in America.
 James Talerico, a former seminary student, teacher and state House member in Texas, and Adam Hamilton, a Christian pastor in Kansas, were gaining ground and giving voice to the intersection of faith and politics.
 Abdul El-sayed in Michigan was poised to become the first American Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.
 Two women doctors, Dr. Amy Acton and Dr. Annie Andrews, stepped forward to run for governor of Ohio and U.S. Senator from South Carolina, respectively. They might have the prescription their states need to protect healthcare.
 Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s Native American lieutenant governor,  mounted a  run for the U.S. Senate—another first for Native women.
 The icing on the cake was when Scott Colom — a moderate Black candidate, former prosecutor in Mississippi emerged as the possible  winner in the U. S. Senate race. A first since reconstruction of 100 years ago. 
 And if that wasn’t enough,  think about some of those who ran down ballot for the U.S. House.
 This included what became known as the 11 Bad Ass women. These women veterans stepped forward as a counteroffensive to the destruction of the U.S. military and the denigration of women. Ten won their seats, including Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral who defeated Lauren Boebert in Colorado.
 Then there was Navy veteran Brett Jones, a gay man who ran for sheriff against a two-term Republican incumbent in Madison County, Alabama. He won.
 And 37-year-old Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who stepped up to run for governor of Alaska. A native Alaskan, he successfully ran for the state legislature at age 23 and hasn’t stopped since. Now he will be the youngest governor in the country, representing rural Alaska and giving voice to rural America.
 More rural voices emerged in Public Regulation and Corporation Commission races across the country. Wendy DeBoer will be the first Democrat on Nebraska’s Commission. In Arizona, two Democrats broke through the all-Republican Corporation Commission to bring new voices to the table. And in Georgia, Democrats won a majority on the PRC for the first time. Data centers and energy costs brought out brave candidates in rural areas.
 Speaking of rural voices, in New Mexico, after years of pushing out rural Democrats, elected some new ones to the Legislature: David Mooney in HD 38, who lives in Radium Springs, and Rikie Gonzales in HD 7, from Tome in Valencia County.
 Watching the election results at the Illinois celebration was much like watching New Mexico’s results. No surprises. Most of the celebration focused on the breadth of the victories across the country. Texas, Georgia, Kansas, Iowa, and on and on.  
 So many of those elected, mostly Democrats, represent firsts in gender, race, and religion that there isn’t enough space to name them all. It wasn’t about Democrats, rather  what was so badly needed in 2026:
 A return to decency, an endorsement of our nation’s diversity, and a desire by the people to protect democracy and have their voices heard.
